text: Lesson seven built the features. This lesson picks a model and proves, rather than assumes, that it's the right one — using validation discipline that would hold up to a skeptical reader.

Three candidates get compared. The naive rank-reversal baseline isn't machine learning at all — it just ranks last week's return and bets on reversal, and it's the bar every model has to clear. The production model is Ridge regression, L2-regularized linear regression with alpha equal to five, chosen for interpretability and resistance to overfitting given there are only eleven cross-sectional names to learn from. The benchmark is a Random Forest, included specifically to test whether nonlinearity earns its complexity.

All three are validated the same way: purged walk-forward expanding-window cross-validation, de Prado style. Training starts on 2007 through 2011, then walks forward one period at a time. Because the forward five-day target creates overlapping labels near each train/test boundary, a five-day embargo purges exactly the labels that would otherwise leak information across that boundary. That produces roughly one hundred eighty weekly out-of-sample evaluation periods across 2012 through 2025.

Each out-of-sample period, we fit Ridge on the training window and compute the Information Coefficient: the Spearman rank correlation between the model's predicted forward-five-day rank and what actually happened. Averaging that IC across all one hundred eighty periods, with a t-statistic, is how we decide whether a model's edge is real or noise.

The result is the deliberate, honest finding this capstone is built around. Ridge's out-of-sample mean IC is about 0.045, with a t-stat near 2.1 — statistically significant. Random Forest's out-of-sample mean IC is only about 0.018, t-stat near 0.9 — not significant. With just eleven names in the cross-section, Random Forest has room to overfit in-sample without the data to back it up out-of-sample. Ridge wins not because it's fancier, but because it's appropriately simple.
Ridge is the model. Next, Lesson 9 turns its predicted scores into an actual tradable signal — tercile sorts, inverse-volatility weights, and a VIX-regime overlay.
